o: An integer n is strictly palindromic if its representation is palindromic in every base from 2 to n-2. The examples show n=9 failing in base 3 and n=4 failing in base 2. The key observation is that no n ≥ 4 can ever satisfy this: in base n-2, the number n equals 1·(n-2) + 2, i.e., the representation "12", which is never a palindrome. So the answer is always false. Constraints (n up to 1e5, up to ~1e5 bases each costing O(log n)) make the honest check feasible but pointless once you see the proof.
k: In base n-2, n is written as "12", which is not a palindrome, so no n ≥ 4 is strictly palindromic.

a.i: Convert n to each base b in [2, n-2] by repeated division and test the digit sequence for symmetry. This directly implements the definition and terminates quickly in practice because base n-2 always fails.
s: For each base b from 2 to n-2, extract digits of n in base b.
Compare the digit list with its reverse.
Return false on the first mismatch; true if none (never happens for n ≥ 4).
a.t: O(n log n) worst case — n-2 bases, O(log n) digits each (in practice stops almost immediately)
a.sp: O(log n) for the digit buffer

a.i: Since n = 1·(n-2) + 2 and 2 < n-2 for n ≥ 4, the base-(n-2) representation of n is exactly "12", which reads differently forwards and backwards. Hence no valid n exists and we can return false in O(1).
s: Observe n mod (n-2) = 2 and n div (n-2) = 1 for n ≥ 4.
Conclude the representation is "12", not a palindrome.

w: Always prefer the proof-based O(1) solution; the brute force is only useful to convince yourself experimentally. This is a classic brainteaser: the constraint range guarantees n-2 ≥ 2 so the base n-2 argument always applies. Follow-up: for which bases is n guaranteed palindromic? (Only trivial ones like base n-1 where n is "11".)
